tweets.text:
While correlations had been increasing during the selloff, Xu says that changed Friday:

Friday’s move was about idiosyncratic risk, not macro: Single stock vol outpaced the increase in index vol on Friday, with the VIXEQSM Index jumping over 11 pts to a 1-year high of 58% (vs. VIX Index up 7pts). 

In other words, expected dispersion increased even as the market sold off almost 4%, as can be seen in the DSPXSM Index rising 5 pts on Friday (see Exhibit 3). 

This comes as investors rotate out of the AI theme into other sectors, rather than selling everything indiscriminately. As tech stocks fall out of favor, Tech vols have risen the most, with QQQ 1M implied vol jumping over 20 pts last week, the most of any global index. In contrast, US small cap volatility, which has very little exposure to the AI theme, saw its volatility trail that of its large-cap counterparts. The RTY-SPX 1M implied vol spread narrowed to a 6-year low of 1.4% as a result.
tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
CBOE's Mandy Xu: Friday’s VIX move, while large, was  surprisingly orderly. The sell-off in SPX® spot (-3.7%) and the  increase in fixed-strike vols (+3.2 pts) accounted for almost  90% of the 7.4pt VIX increase. 

Very little came from demand for downside puts. In fact, changes in skew and convexity contributed just 0.9pt to the VIX move (see Exhibit 2). In contrast, demand for downside protection made up almost half of the Nov 5th VIX spike. This can also be seen in  measures of SPX 1M skew (25-delta ratio), which spiked to  the 95th percentile high after the Nov 5th sell-off but only  steepened modestly to the 80th percentile last Friday. 

Also  notable was the lack of demand for upside calls on Friday, with call skew falling and call convexity unchanged. It seems that while there was little panic on Friday, investors were also not positioning for a quick rebound.

tweets.text: What was your level of pain on Friday?  If 5, 6, or god forbid 7, and somehow you didn't puke perhaps consider the blessing you have received this Thanksgiving week.
tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
In comments in one of my posts I came across a person with no risk target for his portfolio and a view that his job is to maximize return without regard to risk.  I said the job of every investor is to know what their risk tolerance is and hold a portfolio that takes roughly that risk.  Here's my comment

Here's what I do.  You decide if it's useful.  There is a level of change in my wealth that I find to be 1) absolute noise.  There is a level I find 2) slightly annoying.  A level I find that 3) pisses me off but doesn't upset me.  A level that that cause me to 4) loose sleep. A level that causes me to 5)  act to ease the pain.  Those are personal to me.  But I assure you everyone has levels like this.  I have learned that 4 and 5 are not something I am willing to experience.  I have and I don't want to again. So I operate somewhere in the range of 3-4.  Which for me place me at a risk target that I can manage and I acccept the expected return that it provides.  

IF you have never experienced all these levels it's fair to say you aren't taking enough risk but ideally you don't have to experience them and can just imagine them.   The risk of actually experiencing a level 5 event is it could turn into a level 6 event which could be a life changing loss or a level 7 which would be a loss so horrible you could not recover to anything like your current lifestyle. All of those risk levels are out there for you to experience and I encourage you to really understand that and hold a portfolio that takes risk but doesn't allow for 6-7 at all.  Even an unlevered portfolio is shockingly levered when you consider your future liabilities of paying for your lifestyle and your families education etc.

Broadly saw a few issues in the market in early Oct when I shifted defensive.
1. AI demand as evidenced by Frontier revenue deceleration in Q3
2. The downstream impact of (1) on the overall buildout
3. Massive issuance (ANT + hyperscalers)
4. See escalation with Iran as likely
5. Fed has to hike because inflation is bad across entire CPI basket. Ending war helps but doesn’t solve fully

then
6. Dems won House/Senate/TX gov (this was a big swing short because impacts (2))
7. Jensen ousted

Jensen was the cherry on top that made shorting easy. Now he’s back and this helps the AI complex greatly. Off a VIX of 40 last week you have the potential for an explosive bounce, can easily imagine this back in the teens in a few weeks.  

Zooming out, it doesn’t solve the other issues. The market was weak before Jensen was ousted. Once the vol compression and late shorts are squeezed, I still see tough conditions ahead. Sticking with the plan

MIDDLE EAST OIL FLOWS: With data for the first 15 days of November, the trend seen earlier this month is now solidifying: crude oil loadings are down, but a significant part of the drop is offset by rising exports of much needed petroleum refined products. 

*** From what I hear from Persian Gulf officials, the opposite trends in crude and refined products is intentional, with an effort to prioritize the later. *** 
 
@Vortexa puts refined products exports in the first half of November at >4.5m b/d, or about 70% of pre-war level (2025 average). I hear similar numbers from trade houses and national oil companies in the region.

Put crude and refined products together, and Nov 1-15 data suggests overall oil exports are running at the same level of September, but lower than October. Sure enough, Iranian attacks against oil tankers are having an impact, but they are not deterring exporters.

We're thrilled to invest in Embo.

Robots can already do remarkable things in demos, but those skills are fragile. Move an object, change the lighting, or introduce something unfamiliar, and the robot can struggle.

@EmboAI is building the brain for the humanoid workforce. They start by training a world model on massive amounts of video and robot demonstrations so that robots learn general knowledge far beyond what could be collected on their hardware.

Then an agent practices skills inside that model, trying different actions across imagined scenarios and improving through reinforcement learning. The world model provides physical knowledge, and practice turns that knowledge into skills.

Danijar Hafner and Wilson Yan have spent years developing world models together, and their work includes pioneering research like Dreamer and VideoGPT.

Congrats @danijar, @wilson1yan, and the Embo team!

By @venturetwins, @RaghuRaghuram, and @BornsteinMatt
tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
I'm excited to introduce Embo!

We are building the brain for intelligent robots to help people around the world.

We believe intelligent robots will unlock an era of abundance, making goods and services affordable for everybody. But to deploy them at scale, robots need to work out of the box in unfamiliar scenarios. At Embo, we are building frontier AI models with a deep understanding of physical reality and fine-grained motor skills.

Today's robot skills are fragile. Demonstrations can teach repetitive behaviors, but they cannot cover every object or situation a robot will encounter. We need general pretraining at internet scale to fill the gaps between individual tasks and practice to develop reliable motor skills.

The world models our team has pioneered unlock a path to general robots. Our robot brain pretrains on massive amounts of internet video to learn about objects, physical interactions, and how tasks unfold. It then practices motor skills in diverse imagined scenarios to become robust to unexpected situations.

Our team is behind seminal work in AI including Dreamer, VideoGPT, and Diffusion Forcing, with experience from DeepMind, Meta Superintelligence Labs, NVIDIA Cosmos, Berkeley, and MIT.

We have raised a $110M Seed led by @a16z. We are excited to partner with them, @khoslaventures, DST Global, NVentures (@nvidia), @strikervp,  and other strategic investors to bring reliable intelligent robots out into the world.

@EmboAI

tweets.text:
US net equity inflows are up to ~3.0% of GDP, their highest on record in data going back to the 1980s.

Net equity inflows measure foreign purchases of US stocks minus US investors' purchases of foreign equities.

This figure has risen nearly +5.0 percentage points since the 2022 bear market low.

Meanwhile, net debt inflows, which measure foreign purchases of US debt securities, such as Treasuries minus US purchases of foreign debt securities, are down to ~1.8%, their lowest since 2022.

As a result, net equity inflows have surpassed net debt inflows as a % of GDP by the widest margin since the 2008 Financial Crisis.

In other words, foreign investors are increasingly directing money towards US equities rather than US bonds.

Overseas demand for US equities has never been this strong.

As someone that has had their data leaked once before in a breach from another hardware wallet, I am very wary of inputting my home address when ordering hardware devices.

And Trezor have also suffered from its delivery partners having their data leaked, so I think Trezor's new anonymous pickup is the perfect solution for both them as a company and all crypto users.

Across Europe, you can now order a Trezor under an alias, without sharing your home address, and have it shipped in a plain, unbranded box to a pickup location of your choosing. It’s still rolling out across different countries (if checkout doesn't show anonymous pickup, it isn't available in your country yet). The US is expected to follow soon.

Be also wary that when ordering online, paying by card means sharing some personal details with a third-party processor. If you pay in crypto they only receive the txn details.

Imo this should be the option anyone with any material sum of money in crypto uses going forward, and every hardware wallet should offer it by default. You should do your best to never connect your home address with crypto.

tweets.text: Common sense says that you shouldn’t buy any drug that isn’t alcohol/tobacco from a gas station
tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
This is wild...

Big stories in NYT today, where reporters went to an Atlanta gas station convenience store to test cannabinoids and other newfangled, candy-colored drugs. 

They bought a THC joint sold by a company called FVKD Exotics. The packaging lists THC-P and CBG as main ingredients. Testing found neither chemical in the product—but NYT did find an illegally unlisted intoxicant. 

Seeking further information, they contacted the company directly and found the address provided was ... uh, actually a UPS store that had no knowledge of the company.

I don't think you have to be a prude to think that the current state of widespread hallucinogens/cannabis/Kratom productization could possibly use a little more care and oversight. It would nice if the Trump administration were 1/100th as interested in regulating this stuff as they are at outlawing mRNA vaccines.

#Silver $ELEF.TO $SILEF

What does a Bolivian court ruling have to do with a 180 km truck haul?

That’s how far Silver Elephant has trucked silver-bearing rock from Apuradita to someone else’s mill in Potosí. The company wants to build its own mill at Apuradita, and the two other deposits it plans to feed into it are the ones at the heart of the ruling.

As @SilverElMining highlighted below, Bolivia’s Supreme Tribunal overturned the 2024 decision to cancel its subsidiary’s mining contract at Pulacayo and Paca. Paca alone supplied a third-party plant with more than 261,000 wet tonnes averaging 183 g/t silver in 2023–24.

That’s where I see the upside. All three deposits have already supplied outside mills. If Silver Elephant can permit and finance one mill to serve them all, shorter hauls and in-house processing could improve what it earns per tonne.

The next milestone I’m watching is the environmental assessment for the proposed 12,000-tonne-a-day plant. Management aims to file by year-end and expects a licence decision by June 2027.

Disclosure: Paid partnership with Silver Elephant. Please do your own research.

#Uranium $MYRUF $M.CN

Of the 100 companies in my uranium cash table below, Myriad is one I’d watch for a rebound. It reported C$11.54M in cash and equivalents at July 31. Management says it can fund drilling beyond the first 5,000 metres of Phase II at Copper Mountain in Wyoming.

What I like is where those metres are going. Union Pacific drilled roughly 2,000 holes in this district decades ago. The aim is to verify historical results and fill the gaps needed for a first NI 43-101 mineral resource estimate.

the greatest buying opportunities always show up when they seem least obvious.

Collector Crypt's gacha volumes have dropped significantly. so did the solana:CARDSccUMFKoPRZxt5vt3ksUbxEFEcnZ3H2pd3dKxYjp price.

I think a few things clearly aren't priced in, which is why I believe this is one of the most undervalued onchain businesses in the industry right now:

- these charts only show onchain revenue. as the partner network building on their API grows and they verticalize the whole stack, a growing share of the business happens offchain. that's hard to verify from the outside, but in my view the business is doing better than these charts suggest.

- you think Ripmart is priced in. it isn't. people understand the value proposition, but hardly anyone grasps the scale of what's being built. I expect it to onboard a huge number of users within the first few weeks, most of them without even realizing they're onchain. probably the single most important thing for the business and its marketplace, and the market gives it zero credit.

- the indices were announced in the worst possible market and sentiment, so they were mostly overlooked. I'd also argue most people don't yet understand what they'll look like and why it potentially even could grow into their most profitable offering. together with Ripmart they're a gamechanger: they broaden the product suite and make the business less dependent on gacha revenue alone, which has been the biggest question mark for more conservative investors.

to sum it up: even on these sharply lower numbers, they still generate more than $70M in annualized net revenue, with one of the most profitable, obsessed and sharp teams in the space.

on top of that, more than a third of the supply sits in the treasury, and the team has confirmed those tokens only enter circulation for something clearly accretive to the business, like strategic acquisitions.

adjust for that and the effective valuation is around $200M imo. the market is pricing in the worst case for solana:CARDSccUMFKoPRZxt5vt3ksUbxEFEcnZ3H2pd3dKxYjp, a Pokémon bubble bursting and revenue in decline, but none of the biggest catalysts and bull cases.

the most obvious non-obvious opportunity out there imo.

THE DAILY METALS PULSE | MONDAY, NOVEMBER 23
#Uranium #Silver #Gold #Copper

Saturday’s tanker attack near Hormuz put oil at the top of my screen. By 04:23 GMT, Brent was trading at $92.67, just ten cents above Friday’s close. Silver had a much bigger morning.

🥈 Spot silver jumped 4.1% to $42.86/oz and gold rebounded 2.9% to $3,635.80/oz by 07:21 GMT. Traders still priced in a quarter-point Fed hike for December, but bets on a half-point hike had faded. If the dollar and the US 10-year real yield climb in New York, can gold hold $3,600?

☢️ Uranium ended last week near US$90/lb. In Australia, Paladin’s retail share offer opened today at A$7.80. The stock rose 2.9% and still closed at A$6.02. Shareholders could buy the same shares on the ASX for 23% less than the offer price. That’s why I’d wait for the result before counting the extra A$50 million.

🔶 Yesterday I asked how long Shanghai buyers would keep paying up for copper. This morning, as imports arrived, the average premium for immediate delivery fell 42%, from 5,800 to 3,350 yuan per tonne over December futures. LME copper briefly slipped below US$12,000/t.

🌏 India’s factory PMI hit a nine-month high of 56.0. The eurozone reports at 09:00 GMT and the US at 14:45 GMT. I’ll be looking at new orders for clues to copper demand. For gold, the week’s bigger test is Wednesday’s US PCE inflation reading.

Follow @Swedish_Uranium for the next Metals Pulse.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘀𝗼𝗻 𝗶𝘀 𝘀𝗶𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗲: 𝗚𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗗𝘅 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗵𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗮 𝗱𝗲𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺. 𝗜𝘁 𝗵𝗮𝘀 𝗮 𝗿𝗲𝗶𝗺𝗯𝘂𝗿𝘀𝗲𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗰𝗼𝗹𝗹𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝗯𝗹𝗲𝗺.

GeneDx is a leader in pediatric genomic diagnostics. The company helps diagnose rare genetic diseases in children, sometimes ending years of uncertainty for families who have been going from one hospital to another looking for answers.

𝗧𝗘𝗦𝗧𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗩𝗢𝗟𝗨𝗠𝗘𝗦 𝗞𝗘𝗘𝗣 𝗚𝗥𝗢𝗪𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗔𝗧 𝗔𝗡 𝗘𝗫𝗧𝗥𝗔𝗢𝗥𝗗𝗜𝗡𝗔𝗥𝗬 𝗥𝗔𝗧𝗘.

The demand is already there. GeneDx reported 25% year-over-year growth in exome and genome testing volumes in Q3, with full-year growth guidance of at least 28%. Anthony, the "spy" story appears to be as fake as Russiagate. Here are the facts as I understand them.

(1) First, Alice Huang was at a company called Megaspeed[1], which everyone agrees bought Nvidia chips to sell to Southeast Asian companies called neoclouds. This is in itself completely legal under US law.

(2) However, some both inside and outside the admin didn't like this. They want to block Chinese nationals from accessing cloud services with Nvidia GPUs even if those servers are located outside China. Fine, but the so-called Remote Access Security Act (RASA) to block this has passed the House but not the Senate, and is not law[2].

(3) Singapore's government also looked into this when Alice Huang was on their soil[3] and didn't find any evidence that Megaspeed was actually selling chips to China illegally — let alone that she was a "Chinese spy." They did give her an entry ban, but that's like a visa denial.

(4) The related point is that it's not actually illegal to sell Nvidia chips to China! Since the Biden admin, there has been a complex and constantly-shifting set of export restrictions on chips. As of right now, Nvidia is allowed to sell H200s[4] to China, and indeed has designed these to comply with applicable law.

(5) But you know what...China actually also doesn't want Nvidia chips in China [5,6], because they want to build up their homegrown chip industry. The Nvidia chips are so good that China doesn't want to remain dependent on American chips, or vulnerable to possible US backdoors.

(6) The broader point is that this is an argument between nationalists and capitalists. Nationalists argue that US companies shouldn't even get close to selling to China, and shouldn't even be selling to neoclouds, even if it's "technically" legal. Capitalists argue that it's impossible for American companies to dominate world markets without, you know, being allowed to dominate world markets by actually competing in them. Thank you to everyone who joined us in Miami for our inaugural Investing Through the Cycles (ITC) conference.

To the attendees who traveled from all around the world, it meant a lot to me that you made the trip. Some of my favorite moments were between sessions, when I finally got to meet people in person who have been part of the ITC community for years.

To our speakers, thank you for making the time to join us and for sharing how you think about markets. One of the reasons I wanted to put this conference together was to hear from people who can look at the same market and come to very different conclusions. I appreciated how willing you were to explain your thinking and challenge one another’s views.

A special thank you to Dana Howell @thedanahowell  for organizing the conference. Dana thought through so many of the little details that made people feel welcome. I saw how much care went into bringing the weekend together, and I’m grateful for all of it.

I’m glad we got to spend the weekend together, and I hope to see you again next year.

tweets.text: $HYPE price down 35% while revenue up 35%
tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
$hype is cheap again.

the price fell 36% since september. $98 → $62.5. but the revenue didn't.

hyperliquid revenue:

> 90 days before the top: $164M
> last 90 days: $221M (+35%)
> november: $2.6M a day, the highest of 2026

all of it is used to buy back hype. and a lower price means each dollar buys more tokens.

hype bought back:

> 90 days before the top: 2.31M
> last 90 days: 2.73M (+18%)
> november: ~36K a day, the most since march

so for $1 of yearly revenue you now pay:

> hype at the top: $33
> hype today: $17
> cme: $25
> nasdaq: $28
> robinhood: $29

another way to see it: at this pace, buybacks equal 6% of hype's market cap a year. at the top it was 3%. cme gives back ~3.5% to its shareholders.

more revenue, more buybacks, lower price.

on these numbers, hype is undervalued.

I spent the entire weekend digging deeper into the markets, and I need to take back what I said below.

What I’m seeing in currencies, like the BRL and others, has forced me to reconsider. 

I take my market calls very seriously. Historically, when I’ve called a major reversal, I’ve had enough conviction to tell people to go all in. I cannot give you that same level of confidence right now, and I owe it to everyone who follows me to say so.

Yes, futures are ripping, and we could see a powerful bounce. But I now believe there is a very real possibility that the Nasdaq could fall as much as 38% before establishing a long-term bottom.

I remain extremely bullish on what comes after. The next move will be absolutely explosive. But getting there could be much uglier than I previously anticipated.

Trade carefully here.

This outlook applies strictly to equities. I have no opinion about Bitcoin’s near term direction, and I’m not selling a single sat regardless.

I don't like how bullish the bulls are becoming

I also don't like how this bounce looks

I also don't like how everyone is bringing out the "this is the most extreme selling in years!" and "10-sigma event" to justify buying the dip

Generally, I think that you a strong BTFD scenario is made when stocks correct sharply in an irrational scenario and can be argued to be broadly undervalued when you're in an environment that is rather accomodative to stocks - for example, the Iran War, or Liberation Day, both of which were one-off macro events that spooked the market in an otherwise ok-environment at the beginning of the bull run

However, at these levels, if you ask me there is no irrational selling going on here. What is irrational about selling after every stock has done multiples from the bottom? 

My intuition is telling me that it's ok to DCA here for long term positions, and ok to play the bounce, but it is not ok to bet the farm on some sort of V-reversal here - UNLESS we get a major catalyst to justify that ; then yes, I will agree it's extremely +EV to do so

But if nothing changes, and we keep getting the same shit, then it seems pretty meh.

Nvidia's board has listened.

It has been a long 14 days, but we are pleased to see Nvidia's, $NVDA, board agree with our view to reinstate Jensen Huang.

From day one of this controversy, we maintained a firm view:

The door for Jensen Huang to return should never have been closed without a thorough and independent investigation.

Despite the board explicitly ruling out his return just days ago, we remained firm in this view.

The cost of equity capital has also increased materially with the recent substantial decline in the stock market. 

The Fed’s 2% inflation ambition is misguided. Geopolitical risk and the required investment in global military spending, de globalization and tariffs, and the massive AI infrastructure and related energy investment are features of the world that did not exist when the 2% target was set. 3% inflation is a more realistic ambition in the new world. 

The Fed will put the U.S. and world in recession if it continues to raise rates in a failed attempt to drive inflation to 2%. 

Tell me why I am wrong.

tweets.text:
That isn't what End to End encryption means. 

It just means the payload is encrypted on the user's machine, it can travel across several intermediaries until it reaches the endpoint (i.e., privy's servers). 

It is then decrypted by the recipient. 

Importantly, it should _also_ be authenticated, so when the user encrypts the message they know the public key indeed belongs to the recipient (i.e., privy) and not anyone else.

tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
Frontier models can now propose technical social science research designs that experts grade more highly than the world's top political economist's---that's the finding from our new Free Systems eval, SnyderBench, in which we have PhD experts blind grade research proposals from AI models compared to papers written by Harvard political economist Jim Snyder (which the experts have not previously read). 

At the same time, we see no evidence that models can develop research ideas that experts rate as better overall contributions. They're getting better and better at the technical part of research, but not necessarily at the more subjective part.

This could be because human experts possess "judgment" that the models do not. 

It could also be that research "contribution" is so subjective that it doesn't actually point at any meaningful goal---consistent with this possibility, we find that our human experts don't agree with one another when rating project ideas for the strength of their contribution, with agreement rates barely higher than random chance. Perhaps social science research is what @alexolegimas might call a "relational good": something people value in part because it's produced by a human. We're not sure. 

This past January, I released the results of a pilot in which I had Claude Code replicate and extend a past empirical paper on vote-by-mail. 10 months later, it's stunning the amount of progress that's been made. It's no longer interesting to ask whether AI can collect data and run analyses automagically---we take that for granted---instead, the question is how much of the entire research loop AI can complete. Our tentative answer: AI can handle the technical aspects of empirical political economy research from end to end, devising the design and executing it, but for now, we still need humans to drive the agenda. 

This is joint work with @AndyCWMyers, and is of course dedicated to my PhD advisor Jim Snyder, who remains the world's great empirical political economist, AI or no AI. 

Lots more in the full piece here:

https://freesystems.substack.com/p/benchmarking-ais-research-taste-in
